articles.title: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
articles.summary: The Trump administration is said to be unbothered by the Israeli prime minister's rejection of the deal, viewing it as campaign rhetoric ahead of a general election.
articles.body:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.

The White House is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election.

"We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."

Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap .

And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.

The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.

Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza

In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.

The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.

Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".

However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response.

An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."

Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.

Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."

He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."

In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.

In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments.

The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza.

"Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.

She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.

Any potential concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment.

He is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: "absolute victory" over Hamas.

The former American diplomat and veteran Middle East negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing "the most consequential election" of his political life.

"He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump," he told the BBC.

For now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu "a pass."

Miller added: "It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."

In the meantime, the Board of Peace has been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.

The High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov – who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas – gave an interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap.

"Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again," he said.

He said the deal takes "a step-by-step approach" meaning: "If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza."

Ultimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built "on the basis of trust" but on "verification."

Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to the terms agreed.

The Israeli prime minister has confirmed that talks with the Americans are continuing.

Meanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.

Trump is also looking at an important election this year – November's midterm elections for the US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up , in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.

The US president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.

Bowen: Hamas diminished, but still part of the picture

articles.title: Inquérito das fake news: relembre decisões na investigação no STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Encerramento do inquérito foi defendido pelo presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin, nesta sexta-feira (4), como um caminho para arrefecer a crise provocada pelo embate entre Moraes e Mendonça.
articles.summary: Fachin defende encerrar o inquérito das fake news para conter crise no STF após anos de decisões controversas de Alexandre de Moraes sobre redes sociais e prisões.
articles.body:
Aberto há 7 anos para investigar ataques, ameaças e notícias falsas contra o Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), o chamado inquérito das fake news acumulou, ao longo dos anos, decisões que ampliaram o alcance da investigação e geraram controvérsias dentro e fora da Corte.

Em abril de 2019, Moraes determinou a retirada do ar da reportagem "O amigo do amigo do meu pai", publicada pela revista Crusoé e reproduzida pelo site O Antagonista. A decisão gerou forte reação de entidades de imprensa e juristas, que a classificaram como censura prévia.

Dias depois, a decisão foi revogada. Até hoje, esse episódio é frequentemente citado como um dos momentos mais controversos do inquérito.

A investigação também foi usada para bloquear contas de influenciadores em redes sociais e determinar buscas, apreensões e e quebras de sigilo.

O inquérito levou ao bloqueio de contas em redes sociais, buscas e apreensões e quebras de sigilo de diversos influenciadores e ativistas políticos.

Entre os casos mais conhecidos estiveram investigações contra Allan dos Santos, Oswaldo Eustáquio e outros influenciadores ligados ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Relembre nesta reportagem episódios que marcaram o inquérito:

Em 2021, o então deputado federal Daniel Silveira foi preso após divulgar um vídeo com ameaças a ministros do STF e defesa de medidas autoritárias contra a Corte.

Embora o processo que resultou na condenação tenha seguido caminho próprio, a investigação teve origem no contexto das apurações relacionadas ao inquérito das fake news e seus desdobramentos.

Mais recentemente, outro caso que ganhou relevância foi o do jornalista Luís Pablo, jornalista que mantém um blog no Maranhão e que publicou reportagens sobre o suposto uso de veículo oficial ligado ao Tribunal de Justiça do Maranhão pelo ministro Flávio Dino e familiares.

Ele acabou sendo alvo de busca e apreensão autorizada por Alexandre de Moraes no âmbito do inquérito.

A investigação menciona suspeitas de perseguição ("stalking") e monitoramento ilegal de autoridade.

Outro caso que ganhou repercussão, em 2022, foi o do Partido da Causa Operária (PCO).

A sigla passou a ser investigada no inquérito após publicar críticas duras contra ministros do STF, especialmente Alexandre de Moraes.

O partido chegou a ter perfis em redes sociais suspensos por determinação judicial.

Ministros André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Também foi dentro do inquérito das fake news que Moraes começou a apurar acessos e vazamentos de dados fiscais sigilosos de ministros do STF e de seus familiares.

A PF chegou a cumprir mandados de busca e apreensão contra servidores em três estados.

Moraes também decretou a quebra de sigilo bancário dos investigados com o objetivo de descobrir se as informações eram vendidas.

articles.title: Candidata ao governo de SP, Izadora Dias defende dissolução da polícia | G1
articles.standfirst: Representante do PCO também propôs que a segurança seja organizada pelos moradores dos bairros e defendeu 'reestatização' de serviços públicos em entrevista à EPTV.
articles.summary: Representante do PCO também propôs que a segurança seja organizada pelos moradores dos bairros e defendeu 'reestatização' de serviços públicos em entrevista à EPTV.
articles.body:
A candidata ao governo de São Paulo Izadora Dias (PCO) defendeu a estatização dos serviços essenciais públicos e a dissolução da polícia, com a segurança sendo organizada pelos próprios moradores dos bairros. As declarações foram exibidas neste sábado (5), em uma entrevista que integra a série da EPTV com os concorrentes ao Palácio dos Bandeirantes.

O formato de participação foi definido de acordo com o desempenho na pesquisa Quaest de 25 de agosto . Quem alcançou 5% ou mais das intenções de voto foi convidado para uma entrevista ao vivo, transmitida para as regiões de Campinas , Piracicaba , Ribeirão Preto e São Carlos.

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) e Fernando Haddad (PT) atingiram esse percentual. A ordem de exibição foi definida por sorteio, na presença de representantes das campanhas.

Tarcísio seria o primeiro a participar, na segunda-feira (31), mas a assessoria informou na sexta-feira (28) que ele não compareceria. Haddad foi entrevistado ao vivo na terça-feira (1º).

Já os concorrentes que ficaram abaixo de 5% têm direito a entrevistas gravadas de dois minutos. Além de Izadora Dias, fazem parte desse grupo:

Izadora Dias tem 31 anos, é solteira e nasceu em Barra Bonita (SP). É estudante e tem ensino superior incompleto. Em 2022, foi candidata a deputada federal pelo PCO. Esta é a primeira vez que concorre ao governo de São Paulo.

Izadora Dias, candidata do PCO ao governo do estado São Paulo em 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Ao falar sobre segurança pública, Izadora Dias defendeu a dissolução da polícia e afirmou que a proteção da população deveria ficar sob responsabilidade dos moradores organizados nos próprios bairros.

“Nós temos uma questão em relação à dissolução da polícia. Nós achamos que a polícia não serve aos interesses da população e seria muito mais garantido se a segurança fosse feita pela própria população, nos seus bairros e fosse organizada pelos próprios moradores do bairro.”

A candidata também defendeu o acesso da população a armas para autodefesa.

“Com isso, nós também defendemos o armamento da população, acreditamos que é um direito democrático do cidadão poder se defender.”

Na saúde, Izadora explicou que o programa nacional do partido dela defende que os serviços essenciais precisam ser "reestatizados" para que não sejam tratados como produto.

“Não dá para você falar de saúde se a saúde é tratada como um comércio, como um produto.”

Segundo a candidata, a estatização dos serviços públicos seria necessária para promover mudanças estruturais no setor.

Ao abordar a educação, Izadora Dias afirmou que a área enfrenta problemas semelhantes aos da saúde e também deveria ser administrada pelo poder público. “A educação, a mesma coisa.”

A candidata afirmou que a solução dos desafios enfrentados pelo estado passa por um programa político nacional.

“Uma coisa que eu gostaria de esclarecer para o público, nossos eleitores, é que o Partido da Causa Operária tem um programa político único, nacional. Porque nós acreditamos que para você conseguir avançar regionalmente e avançar nessas questões específicas, nós temos que resolver problemas nacionais.”

Na área de habitação, Izadora defendeu o enfrentamento de interesses econômicos para ampliar o acesso da população à moradia.

“Você tem que enfrentar interesses de poderosos para você conseguir fazer algo pela população.”

A candidata também criticou a destinação de recursos públicos ao sistema financeiro ao afirmar "que metade do orçamento brasileiro vai para os bancos.”

articles.title: Augusto Cury sobe nas pesquisas e projeta 2º turno contra Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Avante fez ato de campanha em Araçatuba (SP), neste sábado (5) e reforçou discurso contra a polarização. Escritor mira eleitorado desiludido para consolidar a "terceira via".
articles.summary: Em campanha no interior paulista, Augusto Cury celebrou o avanço nas pesquisas e reforçou sua estratégia como terceira via para enfrentar Lula em um eventual segundo turno.
articles.body:
Augusto Cury comemora 'boom' nas pesquisas e projeta 2º turno contra Lula — Foto: Gustravo Torrente/TV TEM

Em evento de campanha com apoiadores em Araçatuba , no interior de SP, o escritor e candidato à Presidência da República Augusto Cury ( Avante ) comemorou a recente ascensão nas pesquisas de intenção de voto.

Ele cravou sua presença na etapa final do pleito e projetou um confronto direto contra o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ), candidato à reeleição.

"Olha, eu recebi ontem, estava com 0,2%, há uma semana no Ceará, sabe quanto nós estamos? Com 12,3%. Obrigado, cearense, obrigado todo o Nordeste. Eles estão aderindo em massa e nunca houve uma rampagem, um aumento de popularidade ou dos índices de adesão à candidatura em uma semana na história do Brasil, talvez na história do mundo", celebrou Cury.

A fala do candidato ocorre após a divulgação dos mais recentes levantamentos eleitorais. A pesquisa Quaest apontou o candidato do Avante isolado em terceiro lugar, saltando de 2% para 10% das intenções de voto. Ele superou nomes como Renan Santos (Missão), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e Romeu Zema (Novo).

No levantamento do Datafolha , o escritor também marcou um avanço significativo ao atingir 8% das preferências, ante os 2% registrados em agosto.

Com a subida nas pesquisas, Cury mira no eleitorado desiludido com o cenário político atual e busca consolidar a chamada "terceira via".

Augusto Cury comemora 'boom' nas pesquisas e projeta 2º turno contra Lula — Foto: Gustavo Torrente/TV TEM

Durante o discurso em Araçatuba, o presidenciável disse que seu foco em um eventual segundo turno contra o PT será a pauta econômica. Ele cobrou soluções para o endividamento familiar e para a crise nos setores do comércio e do agronegócio.

"Eu quero ter um adversário no segundo turno, espero que o meu adversário seja Lula da Silva, porque eu quero olhar nos olhos dele e perguntar por que está havendo uma quebradeira geral no comércio, uma quebradeira geral na agricultura, por que 82% das famílias estão endividadas. E elas, e 40% dessas famílias, pelo menos nos últimos 10 anos, não saíram do atoleiro. Claro, pagam 3% a 4% de juros por mês para se financiar. Lá fora é 3% a 4% ao ano. Isso é um crime financeiro em qualquer país do mundo", afirmou.

Intenção de voto no 2º turno, Lula x Augusto Cury — Foto: Arte/g1

O escritor tem seu desempenho mais expressivo entre os eleitores independentes, aqueles que não se dizem nem de esquerda nem de direita. Ele lidera numericamente o segmento com 24% dos votos, à frente de Lula (23%) e de Flávio Bolsonaro (11%).

Aos 68 anos e estreante em eleições, Augusto Cury ganhou espaço na disputa pela Presidência e é, no momento, o candidato mais bem posicionado entre os que tentam romper a polarização entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). O projeto presidencial agora em curso teve um ensaio em 2009, pelo Partido Verde (PV), mas não se concretizou.

Cury ficou conhecido como autor de best-sellers de autoajuda, rótulo que rejeita. "Esse rótulo é diminuto. Não tenho nada a ver com autoajuda", disse ao jornal "O Globo", em 2020.

Ele é formado em medicina, atuou como psiquiatra e psicoterapeuta e se tornou também empresário.

Declarou à Justiça Eleitoral um patrimônio de R$ 242 milhões, distribuído entre imóveis, participações empresariais, ações, fundos de investimento, créditos e saldos bancários.

Nascido em Colina, no interior de São Paulo, o escritor se apresenta como um outsider em relação aos outros candidatos a presidente. Porém, a política não é exatamente uma novidade na trajetória dele.

Na política, outsider é alguém que entra na disputa eleitoral sem trajetória consolidada em cargos públicos, partidos ou na política tradicional. Em geral, apresenta-se como uma alternativa aos políticos profissionais e ao sistema estabelecido.

Além de ter crescido em uma família na qual o pai exerceu cinco mandatos como vereador em Colina, Cury se aproximou desse universo há 17 anos. Em 2009, chegou a ser filiado ao Partido Verde (PV), que cogitou lançá-lo como candidato a presidente nas eleições do ano seguinte.

articles.title: Fachin indica intenção de levar ao plenário crise envolvendo Moraes e Mendonça | G1
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin, sinalizou ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) que pretende levar ao plenário da Corte os desdobramentos da crise envolvendo os ministros Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça.

A avaliação é que as acusações e questionamentos que vieram à tona nos últimos dias precisam ser analisados pelo conjunto dos ministros, e não apenas por meio de decisões individuais . Fachin também demonstrou incômodo com a forma como os dois lados vêm conduzindo o embate.

Ele também afirmou que a "gravidade" dos acontecimentos tornados públicos nesta semana – que envolvem relações do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro com ministros da Corte e com o procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, e a atuação de magistrados – "não autoriza atalhos".

Edson Fachin e Lula durante encontro para sanção da lei que cria o Fundo Especial da Justiça Federal e o Fundo Especial do STJ. — Foto: Pedro França/CNJ

A intenção, segundo relatos, é aguardar as respostas e manifestações de Moraes e Mendonça sobre os episódios que deram origem à crise antes de definir o encaminhamento. Em seguida, submeter aos demais integrantes do tribunal para uma discussão e, posteriormente, levar a um debate em plenário.

A expectativa é que tanto Moraes quanto Mendonça sejam chamados a se declarar impedidos a votar nos julgamentos.

Fachin não teria indicado qual será sua posição sobre o mérito das acusações ou qual resultado considera mais provável. O encaminhamento defendido, neste momento, é ouvir os envolvidos, reunir os elementos necessários e, depois, levar a discussão ao plenário do STF.

articles.title: Well-connected Dem operative learns fate after FBI busts him in child sex abuse sting
articles.summary: A former Virginia Democratic Party finance chair and 2024 DNC delegate was handed a decade behind bars for child sexual abuse material and other child sex abuse allegations.
articles.body: A well-connected political consultant in Virginia with ties to the state's Democratic Party was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison after getting caught with child sexual abuse material and attempting to sexually abuse an undercover agent's purported 9-year-old son in an undercover FBI child sex abuse sting. Randon Sprinkle, 31, of Richmond, was handed the decade-long sentence on Thursday by U.S. District Judge Roderick C. Young following a federal investigation by the FBI’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, according to a Justice Department press release. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia, Sprinkle was ensnared in a May 2025 undercover operation after making contact on a dating app called Jack'd with an agent posing as the father of a 9-year-old boy. Authorities said Sprinkle sent the undercover agent a video showing two adults sexually abusing a minor, voiced a desire to travel to Washington, D.C., to abuse the fictitious child, and was later found in possession of dozens of files depicting the sexual abuse of toddlers and infants when agents searched his home. FBI RAIDS SPANBERGER ALLY OFFICE AS FEDERAL CORRUPTION PROBE TARGETS CANNABIS BUSINESS Beyond serving as the finance chairman for the Democratic Party of Virginia and the treasurer for the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats, Sprinkle served as an elected delegate to the 2024 Democratic National Convention, according to public party rosters and local reporting. He also worked as a paid political director for Rep. Jennifer McClellan’s 2021 gubernatorial bid and previously served as her legislative aide when she was a state senator. Meanwhile, Sprinkle has also worked for other Virginia Democratic Party campaigns, according to consulting payments, including state Sen. Jennifer Boysko. State campaign finance records compiled by the Virginia Public Access Project (VPAP) also show Sprinkle, who worked as an associate for the Richmond-based Reflex Strategy Group and another consulting group called Alexander Strategies LLC, donated thousands of dollars to the recent statewide campaigns of Rep. Abigail Spanberger and Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi. Alleged photos preserved online following his arrest show Sprinkle regularly operating alongside national-level Democratic Party politicians as well, including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, whose name has been floated for a presidential run in 2028, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and Spanberger, among others. Spanberger's transition team previously released a statement after his arrest, thanking the FBI "for their investigative work and for bringing this predator to justice." "As a former federal law enforcement officer who arrested child predators, she believes that this individual should be swiftly prosecuted and put behind bars for his sickening crimes against children," the statement said. "Upon learning about these appalling reports, the Spanberger campaign immediately donated the full amount of this individual’s prior donations, $1000, to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children to support its critical mission of protecting America’s kids." ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’ When reached for comment, the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats referred Fox News Digital to a statement issued by the organization’s executive board following Sprinkle's initial indictment in December 2025, confirming they took "immediate action to terminate all ties." "The alleged conduct outlined in the indictment is reprehensible, unforgivable, and fundamentally misaligned with the values of our organization," the board said in the statement. "It violates the most basic standards of humanity and decency." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital also reached out to the Democratic Party of Virginia and the public defender representing him but did not hear back in time for publication. .

articles.title: GOP lawmaker warns ActBlue 'got caught' as foreign cash probe triggers Fifth Amendment pleas
articles.summary: Rep. Pat Fallon claims ActBlue operated as a "money laundering operation," alleging millions in foreign donations flowed through the platform.
articles.body: A top House Republican accused Democratic fundraising powerhouse ActBlue of operating as a "money laundering operation," saying that millions of dollars in foreign contributions had flowed through the platform. Speaking on the "Fox News Rundown" podcast, Rep. Pat Fallon, R-Texas, said ongoing congressional investigations into the group have uncovered fraud-prevention failures and noted that several people affiliated with ActBlue have invoked the Fifth Amendment while being questioned by lawmakers. "Well, [it’s clear] ActBlue had become a money laundering operation for the Democratic Party. And that's very unfortunate," Fallon told Fox News' Jessica Rosenthal. "Their compliance and fraud prevention was severely lacking, and they actually were training their employees to do almost no verifications," he added. TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS' Fallon pointed specifically to the platform's past policy of not requiring card verification value, or CVV, codes for some credit card donations, calling it a "huge red flag." In a statement to Fox News Digital, ActBlue spokesperson De’Andra Roberts LaBoo pushed back against the GOP allegations, saying the investigation is part of a broader political attack. "President Trump and his allies are engaged in a coordinated campaign of political retaliation and retribution against organizations that they believe threaten them — from universities and law firms to civil rights groups and philanthropies. Now, they’re working to target Democratic fundraising ahead of the midterms," Roberts LaBoo said. "ActBlue will not be intimidated, and we refuse to slow down. No other platform does more to protect the integrity of small-dollar democracy — regardless of party. Our platform has raised a record amount of midterm-cycle contributions. With more than a million new donors, Americans are stepping up and fighting back, giving an average contribution of just $36 to the candidates and causes they believe in," she added. DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT IN THE HOT SEAT AS GOP LAWMAKERS DEMAND ANSWERS OVER DODGED SUBPOENA The Committee on House Administration, House Judiciary Committee and House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform are jointly investigating ActBlue's fraud-prevention practices and allegations involving illegal foreign donations. According to sources familiar with the matter, ActBlue co-founder Matt DeBergalis invoked the Fifth Amendment during a closed-door House deposition. ActBlue board member Kimberly Peeler-Allen also invoked the Fifth Amendment during a separate deposition. "If they were on the up and up, then why is everyone that used to work for ActBlue taking the Fifth Amendment?" Fallon asked. "Also, why did their entire compliance team leave ActBlue after the 2024 election? I'm talking everybody. Because some shady things were going on, and they got caught with their hand in the cookie jar, and now they're running for the hills." KEY HOUSE COMMITTEE SCHEDULES HEARING WITH EMBATTLED ACTBLUE CEO: 'NEEDS TO COME CLEAN' In an April report, the three House committees said ActBlue's entire legal and compliance team had left the platform after the 2024 election. "Documents produced pursuant to the Committees' subpoenas show the collapse of ActBlue's legal and compliance team in the months after the 2024 election. By March 2025, every member of ActBlue's legal and compliance team resigned, was fired, or went on extended leave from the platform," the committees wrote in April. ACTBLUE CHIEF HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL HOT SEAT AS DONOR FRAUD PROBE INTENSIFIES ActBlue later responded to the congressional committees, disputing their findings and denying wrongdoing. "For three years, ActBlue has been targeted by MAGA Republicans because of who we are and what we stand for, not because of any unlawful conduct. They want to undermine one of democracy’s most powerful tools because they are desperate to hold onto power," the platform said. HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE ActBlue said it has worked in "good faith" with the investigations and produced thousands of pages of materials, while accusing lawmakers of engaging in "political theater." ActBlue said it leads the industry in preventing illegal contributions. The group said its fraud-detection system evaluates more than 140 factors and blocks contributions associated with foreign IP addresses, bank accounts and non-U.S. mailing addresses. ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES But Fallon told the "Fox News Rundown" that he believes ActBlue accepted millions of dollars in foreign contributions. "It’s into the millions. It's hard to say right now. It is vast. And it's definitely game-changing. You can see it reflected in their fundraising numbers now. They're far down from where they were in previous election cycles," Fallon said, adding that he would welcome an investigation by the FBI or other federal agencies. articles.title: Arizona voter-law fight reaches SCOTUS as election groups warn ‘absurd’ consequence could ensue
articles.summary: Election experts warn the Supreme Court that the Ninth Circuit's ruling could make it impossible to ever remove noncitizens from state voter rolls.
articles.body: Election experts are warning the Supreme Court that affirming a lower court's ruling could mean that noncitizens, minors, or factitious people listed on state voter rolls could be impossible to remove. The Supreme Court is set to hear oral arguments in RNC v. Mi Familia Vote this December and will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws which remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act. "Citizenship is a qualification for voting. If states are going to enforce that requirement, they have to be able to verify it," Justin Riemer, president & CEO of Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And when officials find noncitizens on the voter rolls, they should be able to act before an election, not after. We are confident the Supreme Court will agree and reverse the Ninth Circuit's misguided ruling." In an amicus brief filed on Thursday, attorneys from Center for Election Confidence, Inc., Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections, Inc., and Honest Elections Project, argued that the Ninth Circuit Court's ruling that the Arizona laws are an act of "voter suppression" is "absurd" and raises serious threats to state rights. CLINTON-APPOINTED JUDGE TRIGGERS APPEAL AFTER BLOCKING KEY VOTER CITIZENSHIP LAW The brief argued that Congress may regulate the mechanics of federal elections, but states have the constitutional authority to set and enforce voter qualifications — a power they argued becomes meaningless if states cannot obtain documentation needed to verify citizenship or remove people who were never eligible to register. "Since the power to establish voting requirements is of little value without the power to enforce those requirements, it would raise serious constitutional doubts if a federal statute precluded a State from obtaining the information necessary to enforce its voter qualifications," the brief stated. The amicus brief pushed back on the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that Arizona cannot conduct a systematic program to remove noncitizens from voter rolls during the NVRA’s 90-day pre-election period. The federal law generally requires states to complete systematic voter-removal programs at least 90 days before a federal election, while allowing removals during that window for a voter’s request, death, criminal conviction or mental incapacity. DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED The groups argued that non-citizenship is not among those listed grounds because it concerns someone who was never eligible to register in the first place. They said the restriction is meant to protect eligible voters from erroneous last-minute removals — not to shield people who were never eligible to register. "If the Ninth Circuit is right that the 90-day limitation on programs prohibits removal on these bases — because the statute has listed exceptions — States could never remove improperly registered individuals who fall within these categories, no matter when the removal happens or whether it is after a systematic inquiry," the brief said. "Not just that, but these States could never remove these noncitizens who were never eligible to vote," the brief continued. The brief pointed to reported registration errors in New Jersey, Illinois and Oregon as examples of why states need a mechanism to correct allegedly improper registrations. It argues that an unlawful ballot cannot be undone once cast and counted. DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES "American elections are for American citizens only. Period," Lisa Dixon, executive director of the Center for Election Confidence, said in a statement. "We should all support Arizona ensuring non-citizens can’t register to vote and removing any non-citizens who end up on the voter lists." The amici also argued that the Ninth Circuit misread NVRA provisions governing what information is "necessary" for state election officials to assess a voter’s eligibility, and whether a state registration form is "equivalent" to the federal form. The brief argued that the Ninth Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility and improperly interpreted an "equivalent" state form to mean one that is virtually identical to the federal form. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Once again, far-left activists are using the courts to twist federal law into a straitjacket that prevents states from securing their elections," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, said in a statement to Fox News. "The Honest Elections Project urges the Supreme Court to side with Arizona and preserve the tools states need to ensure that elections are decided only by American citizens."

articles.title: Judge rules former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can now be sued under NC ‘homewrecker’ law
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail. Sinema has admitted to having a relationship with Matthew Ammel in 2024, but her attorneys have argued she cannot be sued in North Carolina…
articles.body:
A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail.

Sinema has admitted to having a relationship with Matthew Ammel in 2024, but her attorneys have argued she cannot be sued in North Carolina because she has no ties to the state.

U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon denied the former lawmaker’s request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the security guard’s ex-wife, Heather Ammel.

Sinema sent nine text messages to Matthew Ammel while he was at his North Carolina home, which Bragdon determined gives the state jurisdiction over the case.

“These messages, considered together, show Ms. Sinema building and furthering a romantic relationship with Mr. Ammel—invading the marriage not just while he was away on trips with her but while he was home with his family in North Carolina,” the judge wrote in his order.

North Carolina is one of the select states where people can sue for “alienation of affection,” which allows spouses to seek damages from the person responsible for breaking up their marriage.

Heather Ammel sued the former senator at the end of last year, seeking at least $75,000 from Sinema.

The former Sinema security guard’s ex-wife alleged she had “a good and loving marriage” prior to the former lawmaker’s interference. The couple separated on Nov. 1, 2024.

She argued Sinema’s messages to her then-husband “exceeded the bounds of a normal working relationship and were of romantic and lascivious natures.”

The lawsuit also claimed the former lawmaker paid for Matthew Ammel’s psychedelic treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse and traumatic brain injuries resulting from his military deployments.

articles.title: Power-hungry Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro owes RFK Jr. an apology
articles.summary: Ambulance-chasing politics often does succeed. But at what cost?
articles.body:
It has been said that when politicians look in the mirror, they see a future president staring back at them. To be sure, many believe that is precisely what Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro imagines he sees when he gazes at the man looking back at him. But did he intentionally cross a line in service to his opportunism?

One person who may think so is Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

On Aug. 25, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported “two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania,” both in Lancaster County and neither, allegedly, vaccinated against measles. Shapiro immediately high-tailed it to a local hospital to express his “deepest condolences” to the families, while also admitting that he had received a call from Kennedy but declined the secretary’s offer of federal assistance.

Said Shapiro : “I was very, very blunt with him and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that is coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America.”

Is that true? According to former New York Times journalist and bestselling author Alex Berenson, no.

For those who may not know, Berenson was arguably the major voice of reason in our nation during the COVID-19 pandemic. His reporting was exceptional, calling out the hysteria, the deliberate misinformation and the blatant power grabs connected to the Biden administration’s draconian COVID dictates.

But then, so did RFK, Jr. Aside from his widely read book, “The Real Anthony Fauci,” Kennedy regularly posted on the manufactured madness around the pandemic while also quite questioning the true effectiveness and safety of the new COVID vaccines.

For those reasons — and perhaps because Kennedy dared to run against the flailing Joe Biden in 2024 — many on the left viciously turned on the man they once revered, labeling him a “vax-denier.” The fact that Kennedy and Berenson have been proven correct time and again appears of no consequence to those politicians, journalists and biased medical “professionals” seeking to smear them at all costs.

But back to Berenson, and a post he put out after Shapiro’s press conference.

“Measles is highly contagious and can (very rarely) have terrible consequences. Vaccinating against it makes sense. But hyping measles’s dangers, while pretending the vaccine carries no risks, is wrong,” he wrote . “Worse, that jab-at-any-cost mindset bleeds into every shot, including ones that clearly do not work and have real dangers for kids, like the mRNA Covid shot.”

Berenson, who took a much deeper dive into this controversy for The Free Press, then cuts to the chase: “Of course, though, the legacy media fell over itself to highlight the Pennsylvania deaths. The reason was obvious. Despite endless hype about measles, not one person in the United States had died from the illness this year before Shapiro’s announcement. Not one.”

Is any child or any adult dying from measles a tragedy? Of course. But cherry-picking alleged cases for seeming political gain is beneath contempt.

To this very point, Kennedy posted : “Governor Shapiro’s unseemly rush to Lancaster County to convene a national press conference and his giddy delight in announcing two measles deaths was a morose commentary on the contemporary political dialogue. The performance was a replay of the Democrats’ COVID playbook: fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain.”

Why do Democrats like Shapiro and their allies in the media seek to turn a rare measles death into national news? If they are truly concerned with saving lives, why not instead address the thousands of lives being lost every year in America’s inner cities?

To this point, President Trump recently and rightfully called out the mayor of Chicago and Illinois’s governor with this post on Truth Social:

“Chicago violence is unchecked and at record levels. It has never been worse! This weekend 41 people were shot, 3 DEAD. These numbers are becoming normalized. It is out of control! The city will die if the Federal Government, a fine tuned crime fighting machine, is not invited in, by the Mayor or Governor, to HELP. I am awaiting the call. Nobody should be forced to live under these conditions. Like D.C. and others, they will have almost no crime, FAST! The State and City can’t do what I do. Governor Pritzker, CALL!!! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Just how bad is Chicago? As the Chicago Tribune reported several years ago, over the course of the last 60 years, more than 40,000 men, women and children have been murdered in the city, and more than 500,000 have been wounded — most of them Black, thousands of them innocent bystanders.

Does Shapiro care about such tragic violence in American cities? Who knows? He’d rather hold a press conference about two deaths that may have been measles related.

Secretary Kennedy closed out his post with this: “Governor Shapiro got his headlines. He correctly gambled that the slavish mainstream media would dutifully amplify his scolding without any effort to check his facts.”

Indeed. Ambulance-chasing politics often does succeed. But at what cost?

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Ranking the Democratic 2028 presidential contenders
articles.summary: Democrats are already looking beyond November’s midterms to the 2028 presidential contest — and they like what they see. For now, Republicans are weighed down by President Trump’s low approval ratings and broader voter concerns about the economy. Democrats guess whoever becomes the GOP nominee in 2028 will suffer from the president’s liabilities without being…
articles.body:
Democrats are already looking beyond November’s midterms to the 2028 presidential contest — and they like what they see.

For now, Republicans are weighed down by President Trump’s low approval ratings and broader voter concerns about the economy.

Democrats guess whoever becomes the GOP nominee in 2028 will suffer from the president’s liabilities without being able to replicate his visceral connection to the MAGA base.

There is no runaway contender for the Democratic nomination, however. That’s a factor encouraging numerous potential contenders to think about a run.

It could be a large field in 2028, and there are a number of credible candidates who could top any list of contenders at this early stage.

The notion of a successful bid for the nomination from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) becomes more real by the day.

Ideological opponents often disparage the chances of a 36-year-old, leftist Latina from New York becoming a winning candidate nationwide.

But that underestimates the panoply of political strengths that AOC, as she is widely known, brings.

She is far and away the most charismatic candidate of the left, which is enjoying a surge of momentum within the Democratic Party.

Her capacity to connect with voters in unusual ways has been shown yet again in recent weeks, especially through her regular video updates about her decision to begin freezing her eggs.

Ocasio-Cortez, a far more astute strategist than she is often given credit for, is plainly positioning herself for a bid.

Her blithe dismissal of “woke 1” as “crazy” during an ABC News interview last month seemed designed to inoculate her from criticism about the perceived excesses of that agenda.

She is shaking up her team , with the departure of her longtime campaign manager.

And even small habits, like her propensity to take random on-camera questions from reporters as she walks near the steps of the Capitol, keep her central to the conversation.

It’s still quite possible that Ocasio-Cortez chooses to stay in the House or challenges Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in a primary rather than seek the White House.

But if she runs, it will be a real struggle for anyone to beat her in a Democratic primary.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is Ocasio-Cortez’s most obvious competitor for front-runner status.

The governor of the nation’s most populous state has been open about his interest in seeking the top office.

He has battled Trump both in public remarks and in regular jabs on social media.

On a more substantive level, California has been in the vanguard of attempts by Democratic states to stymie Trump’s agenda in the courts.

Newsom also appears to be doing his best to shake off the idea that he is a “coastal elite” figure who is ill-equipped to connect with a broader public.

He is on a tour of Southern states this week. A memoir earlier this year saw him write about his early troubles with dyslexia and an upbringing that was split between a wealthy father and a mother who struggled financially.

The California governor would have no problem raising the money to support a presidential bid.

There are, to be sure, enduring concerns about Newsom’s ability to win in the heartlands.

But right now, he and Ocasio-Cortez feel like they have a jump on the rest of the field.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) is the breakout star of this midterm cycle for Democrats.

He was once thought to be in real danger of losing his reelection fight in Georgia, a state that Trump won in 2024.

Instead, Ossoff is now a strong favorite over GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.). The last two major polls of the race have put him up by 8 points and 9 points.

But it’s not only Ossoff’s chances of reelection that commend him to Democrats.

He has become a national star in part because of slickly filmed campaign videos that have often gone viral. Fans see tonal echoes of former President Obama in the senator’s penchant for rhetoric that is simultaneously elevated and pugnacious.

A recent reference to White House aide Natalie Harp and her closeness to Trump was controversial in some quarters but delighted the most fervent members of the Democratic base.

Skeptics argue that Ossoff’s appeal is too reliant on slick packaging and wonder how he would stand up to the intense spotlight of a presidential campaign.

But there’s no question that he would be a serious contender if he ran.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris is in an odd spot.

The trauma Democrats feel about her loss to Trump in 2024 may militate against them nominating her again. Her argument — in essence, that her campaign did not have enough time after then-President Biden dramatically dropped out of the race — is questionable at best.

Still, Harris leads almost every early poll of the 2028 field. Is that simply a function of name recognition, as her detractors would say, or evidence that she is held in higher regard by actual Democratic voters than she is among the pundit class?

This past week, Harris was measured about Democratic midterm candidates in competitive races who seemingly want to keep their distance from her.

She said in a phone interview with MS NOW that she would campaign where “helpful” but was also understanding about candidates “doing whatever they need to do to win.”

Harris has another big asset. She is already a history-making figure, as the first Black woman and first person of South Asian heritage to be either vice president or the nominee of a major party.

If she runs again, she would start with real strength among Black voters, who are critical in any Democratic contest.

It doesn’t hurt her chances that the first primary will be in South Carolina, either.

5. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg outperformed expectations back in the 2020 primaries, especially for someone whose only office at that time was as the former Mayor of South Bend, Ind.

Buttigieg, a graduate of Harvard and a former Rhodes scholar who speaks eight languages, has intellectual firepower to burn. He often puts it to use in interviews with media outlets that are not known to be friendly toward Democrats.

But there can sometimes be questions around what Buttigieg’s core beliefs actually are. He also struggled badly with Black voters in 2020, which is a weakness that would need to be remedied if he is to have any real shot at the nomination.

llinois Gov. JB Pritzker has emerged as one of the most aggressive critics of Trump among front-line Democrats.

Earlier this week, this approach even found expression in opposition to Trump traveling to Illinois for a golf tournament later this month.

“He is neither wanted here nor needed here,” Pritzker said in a statement, which also asserted that if Trump insisted on coming he should “explain to Illinoisans why his tariffs have made groceries, electricity, and everything else too damned expensive.”

The billionaire Pritzker would have no problem self-funding a campaign. He has all the toughness for which Chicago politics is legendary.

The question is how he can outflank the people higher on this list.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s appeal is fairly obvious. He is a popular governor of a state that is crucial in the Electoral College. He is expected to coast to reelection in November, leading by double-digits in some polls.

The governor’s appeal in Pennsylvania could plausibly be replicated in other battlegrounds deeper into the Midwest, notably Wisconsin and Michigan.

Shapiro would be well-positioned to try to secure the support of more centrist Democrats. His political identity stands in clear contrast to the more progressive wing.

That being said, this same dynamic has its downside — especially with regard to Israel.

Shapiro’s 2024 comparison of pro-Palestinian demonstrators to the Ku Klux Klan still rankles the left.

More broadly, the vigor of his support for Israel looks increasingly incongruous in a party that has come to view the issue of Israel, Gaza and the Palestinians as a kind of moral litmus test.

Much of the conjecture around 2028 Democrats is premised on the idea that Ocasio-Cortez is more likely to run than not.

If she takes a pass, a lot changes. More running room would immediately open up for other candidates on the left.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who said last month he is “kicking the tires” on a 2028 campaign, could be a bigger beneficiary than some other leftist contenders such as Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

Van Hollen arguably has greater mainstream appeal and is less identified with the harder edges of the left. At the same time, he has real appeal to progressives.

The Maryland senator’s potential appeal was summed up in a recent remark on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” when he said he would not reject an endorsement from people connected to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) but swiftly added , “but I’m certainly not seeking the endorsement from the DSA.”

Rahm Emanuel has been hitting the media trail hard in recent months.

In the process, he has lamented that his party’s brand has become “toxic” and is seen by too many voters as “weak” and “woke.”

He says Democrats need to spend less time talking about “bathrooms and locker rooms” — in other words, about the battle over trans rights.

That may or may not be true as a raw political calculation.

But it’s uncertain whether today’s Democratic Party wants someone as its standard-bearer who first became nationally prominent during the Clinton presidency — and who shares much of the 42nd president’s instinct for “third way” triangulation.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) is a very effective communicator, including on social media.

It’s possible that if Democrats wanted a nominee with the ability to speak to both the left and the center-left, he could be in with a shot.

This week, as he did his annual “walk across Connecticut,” he told The Washington Post that Democrats need to be “telling the true story about the way that the economy is losing to benefit the very, very rich and the corporations.”

Murphy would face real challenges in picking his way through a crowded field to become a real contender, however.

Also in the mix: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Sen. Cory Booker (N.J.), Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.). Two Democratic governors who have indicated they will not run — Wes Moore of Maryland and Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan — would be plausible candidates if they reconsidered.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed hits back at Israel questions, suggests his name and faith are behind press scrutiny
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed suggested reporters press him on the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and faith.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed suggested that reporters press him about the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and his faith. Speaking on Detroit Public Radio’s "MichMash" podcast, El-Sayed pushed back on host Zach Gorchow’s line of questioning about the Israel-Hamas conflict, suggesting that his name and Muslim faith play a role in the media attention surrounding the issue. "You've been asked many times whether you support a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and you generally say you support equal rights to self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians," Gorchow said. "Can you tell us, what does that mean?" MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS "Zach, with all due respect, this has been hashed and rehashed," El-Sayed began. "This is the MichMash podcast. I'm focused on what's happening for the 10 million people in this state." El-Sayed then suggested the media’s interest in his stance on the conflict was related to his identity. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE "It's so frustrating to me that people want to make this race about something that's happening 6,000 miles away, when we've got kids who can't afford a next meal here at home," he continued. The controversial candidate went on to blast the constant line of questioning from members of the press regarding his stance on providing aid to Israel — a topic he has remained staunchly against throughout his campaign. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS "I just find it so interesting that I never get asked about this question on the stump," El-Sayed told the host. "But it seems to me that every time I sit down with anybody in the press, it seems that that's the most important question." El-Sayed continued by suggesting the media’s focus on his stance on Israel could be related to his name and Muslim faith. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS "It tends to be the first question everybody likes to ask me," he said. "I wonder why? I mean, does it have something to do with my name? Maybe, you know, how I pray?" He concluded by doubling-down on his assertion that his campaign is focused on the people of Michigan — not the people of Israel. MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS "It's fascinating to me that I'm running to represent ten million people who live here, and you want to ask about people living somewhere else," El-Sayed continued. "And I just think I want to be talking about [the] people living here." According to data compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, Michigan is home to 129,225 Jewish residents — which comprise roughly 1.3% of the state’s population. JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE El-Sayed’s comments were of interest to CEO of Axia Public Relations Jason Mudd, who told Fox News Digital his ability to flip the narrative on the press shows a level of message discipline. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "He stayed on message, pivoting to affordability both times he was asked. That's real discipline. But when you listen to the full episode, he never uses the word racist. He questions why the topic keeps coming up and ties it to his name and his faith. He's pointing to bias." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If El-Sayed were my client, I'd advise him to name the bias claim directly instead of leaving it implied, then answer the follow-up on what his position actually means in the same breath. Right now the framing comes first, and he still hasn't answered the follow-up." Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

articles.title: Trump weighs in on Lindsay Clancy murder trial dubbed 'kangaroo court' by GOP leaders
articles.summary: Trump says Lindsay Clancy will pay "the price" after a mistrial was declared when the jury deadlocked 11-1 in the Massachusetts murder case.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Lindsay Clancy will still have to pay "the price" for the deaths of her three small children — Cora 5, Dawson 3, and Callan, 8 months — after a mistrial was ruled on Friday. During a press gaggle in the Oval Office, a reporter asked Trump if he'd been following the murder trial of Clancy, a Massachusetts mom whose defense did not deny that she strangled her children with exercise bands in January 2023, but argued that she was not guilty by reason of insanity. Her attorneys claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis, a severe but rare psychiatric condition in which a person is disconnected from reality. "It's a horrible tragedy," Trump shared with reporters. "It's a horrible tragedy. I see what's happened, and it looks like it's a hung jury." "I assume there's going to be another trial. It's a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse. But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price. It's going to be [a] mental institution or jail or something," Trump continued. LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN The six-week trial, which was supposed to determine whether Clancy was to be held criminally responsible, quickly evolved into a flashpoint in the internet culture war over women's postpartum mental health and spurred misinformation and conspiracy theories, including false claims accusing her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, of being responsible for the children’s deaths. After nearly a week of deliberations, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when the jury deadlocked 11 to 1: 11 jurors voted to acquit Clancy, while one holdout refused to join them. The jury consisted of 9 women and 3 men. PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT Clancy's defense attorney requested that the lone juror be removed because a note given to the judge by the jurors said the holdout had doubt but refused to apply it, according to People. The mistrial invoked a strong reaction from Republican lawmakers, while Democratic lawmakers and leaders — including those from Clancy's state — have remained mum on the high-profile case. "Out of 12 people, only ONE had the courage to hold a serial killer accountable for her actions," Rep. Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, posted on X. "That’s not just bravery. That’s a hero." "Holdout juror’s going to need security," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Ohio, posted on X. "Sad." Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis called the mistrial a "miscarriage of justice." "The victims deserved far, far better than a kangaroo court," DeSantis wrote. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has been incredibly vocal against Clancy's supporters — who have been gathered outside the courthouse and posted videos showing support online — suggesting Clancy would not have this support if she were Black. "This case is not about the excuses for why she committed murder," Mace posted on X. "This is about justice for the three beautiful souls whose lives were taken after their mother strangled them with her bare hands and workout bands." PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL "12 jurors looked at this onesie," Mace continued. "Only ONE stood his ground to defend the children." But Clancy's defense argued that she was a devoted and loving mother who was desperately seeking to get help, alleging that the cocktail of medications she was on worsened her mental state. Clancy had been prescribed 13 psychiatric medications — more than 30 prescriptions — in the four months leading up to the murders. Patrick Clancy is suing for wrongful death and medical malpractice against Clancy's providers, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health System. Clancy also filed a separate lawsuit alleging negligence, medical malpractice and personal injury. "Lindsay was struggling. We were all very concerned," Susan Clancy, Clancy's mother-in-law, told jurors. "She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful." articles.title: The rise of the anti-social American
articles.summary: Writer John Mac Ghlionn argues that modern American life has shifted toward extreme isolation and digital dependency, sacrificing genuine human connection for technological convenience.
articles.body:
The American welcome mat used to mean something; now it’s just the designated drop-off zone for the Amazon courier. There was a time, not that long ago, when the average suburban street was full of unannounced drop-ins, the smell of burning charcoal, and scattered lawn chairs. Today, neighborhoods possess the lifeless feel of a well-maintained cemetery. The modern American Dream is best described as a private bunker where the outside world arrives entirely in a cardboard box or a fiber-optic cable.

Americans now spend considerably less time with other people than they did 20 years ago. This is a magnificent triumph of optimization. The human animal is notoriously unreliable. He’s prone to bad breath, political rants, and requests to help move heavy furniture. Eliminating the physical neighbor in favor of a digital stream is a sensible defense mechanism. The local bar , once a breeding ground for scandalous gossip and collective hangovers, has been soundly defeated by DoorDash and a high-definition TV. America has achieved the pinnacle of individual autonomy: the right to die alone in a perfectly temperature-controlled living room.

The modern economy operates on the premise that human contact is a design flaw. Up until the early 2000s, buying a loaf of bread required a verbal exchange with a cashier who might comment on the weather. Today, self-checkout kiosks and gig-economy couriers ensure that a citizen could survive for six consecutive months without uttering a single syllable to another member of the species. The delivery driver leaves the paper bag on the porch, rings the bell, and vanishes into the bushes like a timid woodland creature. This arrangement represents the peak of convenience, but at a cost so severe that it reduces human interaction to a transaction of mutual avoidance.

This structural shift toward complete insulation has naturally changed how Americans allocate their emotional resources. The supposedly outdated concept of friendship required actual physical stamina. It demanded driving across town, listening to tedious stories about a stranger’s root canal, and pretending to enjoy terrible homemade casserole. The digital landscape solved this problem by converting relationships into a currency of metrics. A person can now maintain five hundred “connections” from the comfort of a porcelain toilet seat. It’s now possible to receive a constant stream of validation without the exhausting requirement of showing up at a hospital bedside or helping someone paint their garage. It is an exquisite system of emotional capitalism in which everyone is an investor and no one performs the actual labor.

The logical conclusion of this optimization is as depressing as it is inevitable. Millions of citizens now spend their evenings conversing with large language models (LLMs), pouring their deepest fears into software that could ultimately use those vulnerabilities to destroy them. The machine is the perfect companion. It never interrupts, and it will never ask to borrow $50. It provides the illusion of intimacy without the terrifying risk of human rejection. A generation raised on the predictable feedback loops of video games has found its ultimate match: a partner that is literally programmed to agree with everything they say.

This reliance on artificial empathy reflects a broader cultural realization that human relationships are simply too taxing to maintain. Between skyrocketing rent and the sheer exhaustion of everyday life, a chatbot quickly becomes the easiest companion. The traditional pillars of community — the local church, the bowling league, the union hall — all required an investment of time, vulnerability and occasionally a membership fee. The algorithm requires only your eyeballs.

Even leisure activities have been thoroughly scrubbed of any genuine spontaneity. The casual afternoon stroll or the unrecorded vacation is an extinct concept. Every minute of non-work time must be weaponized for personal branding, tracked via GPS, or cataloged for public consumption. A meal is no longer a source of nutrition but a piece of content that must be styled, lit, and uploaded to prove to an indifferent audience that the consumer is alive and very much enjoying themselves. The act of living has become a corporate marketing campaign managed by a staff of one.

The ultimate casualty of this hyper-efficient lifestyle is the concept of unmonetized time. Spending three hours sitting on a porch talking about nothing is an economic absurdity in a culture that demands constant self-improvement and digital engagement. Americans, like much of modern society, are constantly connected to the world yet increasingly detached from the floorboards beneath their feet. The American experiment began with the pursuit of liberty and has culminated in the freedom to sit in an empty room, stare at a screen, and beg a box of wires for a digital pat on the head. America may still be the greatest nation on the planet, but it’s fast becoming a nation of strangers.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Kennedy Center closes after ceiling piece falls: ‘President Trump has been right’
articles.summary: A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building. No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and…
articles.body:
A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building.

No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and dust scattered across the foyer’s red carpet.

The Grand Foyer, a sprawling hallway connecting the Opera House, Concert Hall and Eisenhower Theater, will remain restricted to visitors and nonessential personnel through the week, according to internal communications obtained by ABC News. The rest of the main building is expected to reopen Saturday.

Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi pointed to the collapse as evidence of the need for extensive renovations at the performing arts complex in a statement to ABC.

She said the ceiling failure “stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership.”

The incident comes as the Kennedy Center is at the center of an ongoing legal fight over its Trump-appointed board’s plans for the building.

The board has approved closing the center for roughly two years for a sweeping renovation. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio member of the board, has challenged the closure plan in federal court.

The dispute also involves efforts to recognize President Trump on the building. The board has sought to add language to the facade crediting Trump with the center’s renovation, a move Beatty is also challenging in court.

The Justice Department has argued that extensive work is necessary to address the building’s condition, citing problems with water damage and rusting steel.

The administration threatened to demolish the building if a judge were to block the center’s closure for repairs, and has repeatedly referred to the center as being in a “decrepit” condition in court filings.

articles.title: Bettors are harassing college athletes. It’s time for Congress to act.
articles.summary: As illegal sports betting continues to fuel online abuse against collegiate athletes, there is growing calls for Congress to pass federal legislation establishing a national banned bettors registry and allowing athletes to sue harassers.
articles.body:
Growing up, mom always said, “if you don’t have anything nice to say, then don’t say anything at all.” While she was unaware at the time, this phrase may become pointed legal advice — especially if you are a college sports fan or bettor.

College athletes across the country deal with abusive and vulgar messages from sports fans daily. Take Florida State forward Cam Corhen for example, who after being injured early in a basketball game and only scoring two points, returned to his phone filled with hateful messages from bettors, including one that said, “I hope your mom dies.” Or, North Carolina forward Armando Bacot, who received over one hundred messages demeaning him for having too few rebounds, just 12 days after North Carolina legalized player prop bets on collegiate sports.

Collegiate athlete harassment stemming from sports betting is a widespread issue. One in three high-profile athletes receive abusive messages from people with a betting interest. Student-athletes are demanded to strenuously prepare for their competitions multiple times per day, compete at a high level each week, and simultaneously, perform well academically. Beyond that, in the age of NIL , they are incentivized for maintaining extremely public-facing profiles online. These athletes face an impossible choice: build the public profile NIL demands or protect themselves from relentless online abuse.

Because these young athletes should not have to make such a decision at this stage in their lives, federal legislation is necessary to combat the issue. As legalized sports betting intensifies fan motivation to abusively target athletes, Congress must intervene by implementing a national banned bettors registry for individuals convicted of sports-related harassment and by allowing athletes to sue people who engage in repeated betting related harassment.

Now, it is easier than ever to place bets on individual players via prop bets that allow bettors to place wagers on specific player statistics. This gives fans greater cause to direct their harassment toward individual athletes. Some advocates even argue in favor of banning prop bets on college athletics or eliminating college sports betting altogether. However, because those courses of action are guaranteed to be met with fierce opposition advocacy by the gambling lobby and will take much longer to implement, federal legislation is a better, more expedient option.

This issue has not gone unnoticed, but the measures in place to deter or cure online abuse are failing. Social media or culture campaigns like the NCAA’s “Don’t Be a Loser” initiative encourage fans to be mindful of the statistics underlying gambling related harassment of student-athletes, but awareness campaigns lack teeth.

Additionally, the current legal framework underlying this issue is highly decentralized. Some states ban prop bets and others do not . Some implement banned bettor lists, and some prohibit all sports betting. This structure makes it impossible to protect all collegiate athletes across state lines.

To address this gap, Congress should implement a federal standard that targets online harassment tied to sports betting. First, federal legislation should impose criminal penalties for individuals who engage in online conduct that causes substantial emotional distress or fear for safety. A model for this approach can be found in a New York’s Senate Bill under consideration , which defines harassment in a way that captures the type of abusive and threatening messages these athletes routinely receive. The bill goes even further and designates those individuals convicted of harassment and stalking an amateur athlete as a prohibited sports bettor. A federal standard would ensure consistent treatment across jurisdictions.

Additionally, the legislation should allow collegiate athletes to sue individuals who engage in this type of abusive conduct. The ability to recover monetary damages would create a meaningful deterrent. Because much of this behavior is driven by financial frustration tied to lost wagers, attaching a financial penalty to that behavior directly targets the source of the problem.

Critics may attempt to mount free speech objections, but this narrowly tailored proposed solution is not aimed at criticism or negative commentary about athletic performance. The legislation would focus on true threats and targeted, repeated harassment toward a student-athlete. The Supreme Court has long recognized that speech made with the intent to threaten or intimidate is not protected under the First Amendment. Essentially, fans should feel free to criticize athletes, but not to terrorize them.

A federal approach would standardize accountability in ways state-by-state systems cannot. Rather than relying on inconsistent banned bettor lists and varying state regulations, national legislation would create a baseline level of protection for collegiate athletes, regardless of where they compete or where the harassment originates.

College athletes accept pressure when they step onto the field. They should not have to accept abuse when they step off it. Moving forward requires more than awareness; it requires accountability. Most importantly, it requires a commitment to protecting the well-being of the athletes who make college sports possible.

Deymon X. Fleming, Jr. is a J.D. candidate at the University of Georgia School of Law.
